claims.text: The new approach can decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit site-specific force constants, local lattice distortions, anharmonicity, and impurity scattering provide the physical basis for separating phonon and electronic transport.
Randomly distributed principal elements and oxygen impurities create local lattice distortions that alter phonon-scattering rates and mediate lattice thermal transport.
Defect-free, oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr has an intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity approximately 30% above conventional Debye-based estimates from 300 to 1200 K.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are nearly equal.
Oxygen-induced scattering reduces the total thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr containing about 1 wt.% oxygen to 10–17 W/(K·m).
Earlier Debye-based or average-force-constant models fail to capture the full atomic-scale disorder and impurity effects in HfNbTaTiZr.
The target pristine sample is high-purity, nearly stoichiometric, defect-free, and negligibly contaminated by oxygen.
Additive manufacturing can produce bulk HfNbTaTiZr while minimizing extrinsic defects.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be synthesized in nearly fully densified bulk form by printing, debinding, and vacuum sintering.
HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen are experimentally realizable.
Single-phase HfNbTaTiZr samples are experimentally realizable.
The predictive advantage will diminish in polycrystalline samples with substantial grain-boundary scattering.
Extrinsic scattering dominates when defect concentrations are uncontrolled or oxygen content exceeds approximately 1 wt.%.
Local force-constant and scattering-rate variations produce approximately ±10% uncertainty in the predicted 30% enhancement.
Cryogenic time-domain thermoreflectance or magnetic-field modulation can distinguish lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions over the proposed measurement range.
Failure of oxygen-free samples to exceed Debye-based lattice-conductivity predictions by approximately 30%, allowing ±15% variability, would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K and lattice dominance above 300 K would falsify the hypothesis.
